name: Media & Society
description: An elective course examining the complex relationships between mass media and society, exploring how media shapes and reflects culture, politics, identity, and democracy.

modules.title: Media's Role in Society
modules.objectives: Explain the major social functions of mass media; evaluate how media simultaneously reflects and shapes social values and norms. Students will interpret sources or examples, explain cause-and-effect relationships, and support claims with evidence in the module assignment.
modules.readingNote: Understanding Media and Culture §1.1 — mass media, culture, and reciprocal influence
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video — Media's Role in Society; use with the supplied fictional media case
modules.practiceNote: Use the section’s review/exercise prompts to identify the concept before applying it to the supplied assignment case
modules.assignment: Analyze this fictional event packet about a week-long heat emergency. Local TV leads with safety instructions and hourly temperatures; a newspaper investigates which neighborhoods lack cooling centers; a community social account matches volunteers with older residents and repeats unverified shelter rumors. Write 400–500 words explaining how each medium performs surveillance, correlation/interpretation, cultural transmission, or community coordination. Submit: a three-row evidence table plus analysis. Include: one benefit, one risk, and one concrete detail from each supplied summary. Evaluation: 100% total — concept accuracy 30%, evidence 30%, comparison 25%, clarity 15%.

modules.title: Media Literacy
modules.objectives: Apply media literacy frameworks to critically evaluate media messages; identify ownership, purpose, and audience in any media text.
modules.readingNote: Understanding Media and Culture §1.7 — media-literacy questions, purpose, values, and audience
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video — Media Literacy; use with the supplied fictional media case
modules.practiceNote: Use the section’s review/exercise prompts to identify the concept before applying it to the supplied assignment case
modules.assignment: Apply five media-literacy questions to these supplied fictional messages: (A) a beverage ad shows athletes celebrating and says “Fuel your future”; (B) a news brief cites a city report but omits residents affected by a closure; (C) a creator post praises a study app and marks the post “paid partnership.” Submit: a 15-cell analysis table plus a 300-word conclusion. Include: purpose, techniques, included/omitted viewpoints, audience differences, and evidence needed before trusting each claim. Do not visit or contact real accounts. Evaluation: 100% total — framework completeness 35%, evidence-based analysis 35%, verification plan 20%, clarity 10%.

modules.title: Agenda-Setting & Framing
modules.objectives: Explain agenda-setting and framing theories; analyze how media coverage influences which issues the public considers important and how they interpret them.
modules.readingNote: OpenStax Introduction to Political Science §12.1 — gatekeeping, agenda-setting, and framing in political media
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video — Agenda-Setting & Framing; use with the supplied fictional media case
modules.practiceNote: Use the section’s agenda-setting and framing examples to label each choice in the supplied comparison before writing
modules.assignment: Compare two fictional reports about the same housing proposal. Outlet North headline: “City acts to ease housing shortage”; lead emphasizes 600 new units and quotes planners. Outlet South headline: “Neighborhood faces high-rise disruption”; lead emphasizes traffic and quotes homeowners. Both report the same 7–2 council vote. Write 400 words distinguishing agenda-setting from framing. Submit: an annotated comparison plus analysis. Include: four framing choices involving headline, source selection, problem definition, and omitted information. Evaluation: 100% total — theory accuracy 30%, textual evidence 35%, comparison 25%, clarity 10%.

modules.title: Cultivation Theory
modules.objectives: Explain George Gerbner's Cultivation Theory and the mean world syndrome; evaluate empirical evidence for media's long-term effects on worldview.
modules.readingNote: Understanding Media and Culture §2.2 — cultivation and other media-effects theories
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video — Cultivation Theory; use with the supplied fictional media case
modules.practiceNote: Use the section’s review/exercise prompts to identify the concept before applying it to the supplied assignment case
modules.assignment: Use this fictional teaching dataset: a crime drama’s ten episodes show 18 violent incidents, solve 90% of cases, and portray strangers as offenders in 70% of cases; a city statistical summary reports violent incidents are 8% of recorded offenses, case clearance is 45%, and most victims know the offender. Write 400–500 words applying cultivation theory and mean-world syndrome. Submit: a comparison chart plus analysis. Include: three numerical contrasts, a plausible cultivated belief, and a limitation—this small fictional dataset cannot prove audience effects. Evaluation: 100% total — data accuracy 30%, theory application 35%, limitation 20%, clarity 15%.

modules.title: Social Learning from Media
modules.objectives: Apply Albert Bandura's Social Learning Theory to media effects; analyze how observational learning from media influences attitudes and behaviors.
modules.readingNote: OpenStax Psychology 2e §6.4 — Bandura, observational learning, modeling, vicarious reinforcement, and vicarious punishment
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video — Social Learning from Media; use with the supplied fictional media case
modules.practiceNote: Use the section’s modeling sequence and vicarious-consequence examples to complete the supplied mechanism chart
modules.assignment: Analyze this fictional media-modeling case: a popular series shows a student publicly humiliating classmates, receiving laughs and higher status in early episodes, then losing friends and apologizing later. Using Bandura’s attention, retention, reproduction, motivation, and vicarious reinforcement concepts, explain what different viewers might learn at each stage. Submit: a five-part mechanism chart plus 350-word analysis. Include: both rewards and consequences, one protective contextual factor, and no personal disclosure. Evaluation: 100% total — theory accuracy 35%, sequence analysis 30%, nuance/limits 20%, clarity 15%.

modules.title: Media & Political Life
modules.objectives: Analyze how media coverage shapes political knowledge, participation, and candidate image; evaluate the role of media in democratic discourse.
modules.readingNote: OpenStax Introduction to Political Science §12.1 — free press, watchdog role, news values, gatekeeping, agenda-setting, and framing
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video — Media & Political Life; use with the supplied fictional media case
modules.practiceNote: Use the section’s news-value and agenda-setting concepts to interpret the supplied election-coverage data
modules.assignment: Use this fictional three-day election-coverage table: Outlet A devotes 60% of stories to polls/strategy, 25% to policy, 15% to candidate biography; Outlet B uses 20% polls/strategy, 60% policy, 20% biography. Outlet A quotes campaign staff in 8 of 10 stories and issue experts in 1; Outlet B quotes campaign staff in 3 and experts in 6. Write a 400-word analysis of story selection, source selection, agenda-setting, and possible effects on political knowledge. Submit: one chart and analysis. Include: four numerical comparisons, one framing choice, and one claim the data cannot establish. Evaluation: 100% total — data accuracy 30%, concept application 35%, causal caution 20%, clarity 15%.

modules.title: Media & Consumer Culture
modules.objectives: Analyze how advertising and media have created and sustained consumer culture; evaluate the relationship between media content, brand messaging, and consumerism.
modules.readingNote: Understanding Media and Culture §12.1 — advertising appeals and consumer culture
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video — Media & Consumer Culture; use with the supplied fictional media case
modules.practiceNote: Use the section’s review/exercise prompts to identify the concept before applying it to the supplied assignment case
modules.assignment: Analyze this supplied one-hour fictional ad log: 8 beauty ads use aspirational/status appeals, 6 food ads use comfort/emotion, 4 game ads use scarcity/FOMO, and 2 public-service ads use fear. Calculate category percentages and select one ad type for closer analysis. Submit: calculations, a chart, and 350-word reflection. Include: target audience, constructed need, identity promise, and missing information. Do not track your own browsing or share personal data. Evaluation: 100% total — calculations 25%, advertising analysis 40%, evidence 20%, clarity 15%.

modules.title: Gender in Media
modules.objectives: Analyze how gender is constructed and represented in mainstream media; evaluate the social consequences of gender stereotypes and idealized images in advertising and entertainment.
modules.readingNote: Understanding Media and Culture §9.2 — television, representation, and cultural norms
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video — Gender in Media; use with the supplied fictional media case
modules.practiceNote: Use the section’s review/exercise prompts to identify the concept before applying it to the supplied assignment case
modules.assignment: Examine three fictional advertisements: a toy-engineering kit shows only boys building; a cleaning product shows a father and daughter sharing chores; a car ad equates masculinity with aggression and emotional silence. Write 450 words analyzing which gender norms each text reinforces or challenges, likely audience interpretations, and one revision that broadens representation without tokenism. Submit: a three-row representation table plus analysis. Include: specific visual/message evidence and one limitation of inferring audience effects from content alone. Evaluation: 100% total — concept accuracy 30%, evidence 30%, revision quality 25%, clarity 15%.

quizQuestions.question: Which of the following is a social function of mass media?
options: Generating profit for shareholders
Socialization — transmitting cultural norms and values across society
Guaranteeing access to all information regardless of privacy
Replacing all face-to-face communication
quizQuestions.answer: Socialization — transmitting cultural norms and values across society
quizQuestions.explanation: One of mass media's key social functions is socialization — transmitting shared cultural norms, values, and social expectations across generations and communities.

quizQuestions.question: The idea that media simultaneously reflects AND shapes society refers to:
options: The gatekeeper effect
The two-way relationship between media and culture
The direct effects model of media influence
The propaganda model of mass communication
quizQuestions.answer: The two-way relationship between media and culture
quizQuestions.explanation: Media reflects existing social values while also shaping new norms and attitudes — a dynamic, bidirectional relationship between media systems and society.

quizQuestions.question: During an emergency, a local station reports shelter locations while a newspaper explains why some neighborhoods lack services. Together these examples show media performing:
options: Surveillance and correlation
Only entertainment
Only cultural transmission
No social function because the formats differ
quizQuestions.answer: Surveillance and correlation
quizQuestions.explanation: Reporting immediate conditions is surveillance; interpreting causes and relationships is correlation.

quizQuestions.question: Short response: Define or explain: Media's 'correlation' function refers to its role in.
quizQuestions.answer: Media's correlation function refers to interpreting events, connecting information, and helping audiences make sense of what news and social issues mean.
quizQuestions.explanation: Correlation is different from surveillance. Surveillance gathers information; correlation organizes and explains it for the public.

quizQuestions.question: Which of the following is the best example of applying media literacy skills?
options: Accepting a news story as true because it appears on a well-known website
Checking the original source of a claim before sharing it
Sharing emotional stories quickly to help spread important information
Trusting news stories more when they have many comments
quizQuestions.answer: Checking the original source of a claim before sharing it
quizQuestions.explanation: Media literacy involves critical evaluation of sources and claims, including tracing information to original, credible sources before accepting or sharing it.

quizQuestions.question: The question 'who created this message?' in media literacy is important because:
options: Knowing the creator's identity prevents copyright violations
Every message is constructed by someone with a particular perspective, purpose, or interest
Creator identity determines whether the content is legal
Messages created by unknown authors are always false
quizQuestions.answer: Every message is constructed by someone with a particular perspective, purpose, or interest
quizQuestions.explanation: Identifying who created a message helps evaluate potential biases, interests, and perspectives that shaped how the message was constructed.

quizQuestions.question: In media literacy, 'point of view' analysis asks:
options: From whose perspective is this story told, and whose voices are missing?
At what camera angle was the image taken?
What political party produced this content?
Is this content written in first or third person?
quizQuestions.answer: From whose perspective is this story told, and whose voices are missing?
quizQuestions.explanation: Point of view analysis examines whose perspectives are represented in media content and, critically, whose perspectives are absent or marginalized.

quizQuestions.question: A news story quotes officials but not residents affected by a closure. Which media-literacy question is most useful?
options: What viewpoints are represented or omitted?
How many words are in the story?
Is the outlet’s logo attractive?
Did the story use a photograph?
quizQuestions.answer: What viewpoints are represented or omitted?
quizQuestions.explanation: Examining represented and omitted perspectives helps reveal how construction choices shape a message.

quizQuestions.question: Agenda-setting theory was developed through research on:
options: The effect of television violence on children's behavior
The relationship between what media covers and what the public thinks is important
How advertising shapes consumer purchasing decisions
The ways social media algorithms create echo chambers
quizQuestions.answer: The relationship between what media covers and what the public thinks is important
quizQuestions.explanation: McCombs and Shaw developed agenda-setting theory through their Chapel Hill study, finding that media emphasis on certain issues corresponded with what voters considered the most important issues.

quizQuestions.question: Attribute agenda setting asks whether media emphasis influences:
options: Which attributes audiences associate with an issue
When audiences are legally permitted to discuss an issue
Whether every audience member adopts the same policy position
Where journalists are physically located
quizQuestions.answer: Which attributes audiences associate with an issue
quizQuestions.explanation: Attribute agenda setting examines which characteristics of an issue or actor become salient; it is related to, but not identical with, framing theory.

quizQuestions.question: Framing an immigration story as an 'economic opportunity' versus a 'national security crisis' is an example of:
options: Agenda-setting at the first level
Media framing shaping interpretation of the same event
Objective reporting of two different aspects of immigration
Both frames being equally accurate and unbiased
quizQuestions.answer: Media framing shaping interpretation of the same event
quizQuestions.explanation: These two frames emphasize very different aspects of the same issue — economic benefits vs. security threats — shaping audience interpretation and emotional response differently.

quizQuestions.question: Short response: Complete this statement: A newspaper that dedicates its front page to celebrity gossip over international news is exercising which media power...
quizQuestions.answer: The newspaper is exercising agenda-setting power by deciding which topics receive the most attention and prominence.
quizQuestions.explanation: Front-page placement tells readers what the outlet treats as important, even before readers interpret the story itself.

quizQuestions.question: George Gerbner developed Cultivation Theory through research analyzing:
options: The economic structure of the film industry
The content of television programs compared to audience worldview beliefs
The purchasing behavior of heavy radio listeners
Social media algorithms' effects on political opinions
quizQuestions.answer: The content of television programs compared to audience worldview beliefs
quizQuestions.explanation: Gerbner's research at the Annenberg School analyzed the content of television programming and compared it to what heavy vs. light TV viewers believed about the real world.

quizQuestions.question: According to Cultivation Theory, heavy viewers of crime dramas are MOST likely to:
options: Become more empathetic toward crime victims
Overestimate the amount of crime in society
Develop a desire to pursue a career in law enforcement
Believe that the justice system effectively punishes criminals
quizQuestions.answer: Overestimate the amount of crime in society
quizQuestions.explanation: Cultivation Theory predicts that heavy exposure to crime-heavy TV content leads viewers to perceive the world as more crime-ridden than reality — the 'mean world syndrome.'

quizQuestions.question: The difference between 'first-order' and 'second-order' cultivation effects is:
options: First-order effects are immediate; second-order effects take years to develop
First-order effects involve specific facts (e.g., crime rates); second-order effects involve broader worldview beliefs
First-order effects affect children; second-order effects affect adults
First-order effects are caused by TV; second-order effects are caused by social media
quizQuestions.answer: First-order effects involve specific facts (e.g., crime rates); second-order effects involve broader worldview beliefs
quizQuestions.explanation: First-order cultivation effects are specific beliefs (e.g., overestimating crime rates); second-order effects are broader worldview attitudes (e.g., general distrust, fear of strangers).

quizQuestions.question: Cultivation Theory is most applicable to which type of media consumption?
options: Brief, occasional exposure to diverse media types
Long-term, heavy consumption of a single medium (especially television)
Interactive social media use involving real-time discussion
News consumption through multiple credible sources
quizQuestions.answer: Long-term, heavy consumption of a single medium (especially television)
quizQuestions.explanation: Cultivation effects develop through long-term, repetitive exposure to consistent media messages — most studied in the context of heavy television viewing over extended periods.

quizQuestions.question: Albert Bandura's Social Learning Theory proposes that people learn behaviors by:
options: Only experiencing rewards and punishments directly
Observing and modeling the behavior of others
Receiving formal instruction from authority figures
Being genetically predisposed to certain behaviors
quizQuestions.answer: Observing and modeling the behavior of others
quizQuestions.explanation: Social Learning Theory holds that people learn through observation of others' behavior, noting consequences, and modeling behavior accordingly — without requiring direct personal experience.

quizQuestions.question: For social learning from media to occur, which of the following is NOT required?
options: Attention — noticing the modeled behavior
Retention — remembering the behavior
Physical practice — personally performing the behavior to a high standard
Motivation — having a reason to imitate the behavior
quizQuestions.answer: Physical practice — personally performing the behavior to a high standard
quizQuestions.explanation: Bandura's social learning model requires attention, retention, reproduction (ability to perform), and motivation. However, perfect physical practice is not a prerequisite for learning through observation.

quizQuestions.question: A viewer sees a character rewarded for helping a stranger and later imitates that behavior. The reward is an example of:
options: Vicarious reinforcement
Cultivation
Prior restraint
Agenda setting
quizQuestions.answer: Vicarious reinforcement
quizQuestions.explanation: Observing a model receive a reward can increase motivation to reproduce the modeled behavior.

quizQuestions.question: A viewer remembers a modeled behavior but sees the model punished and decides not to imitate it. This best illustrates:
options: Vicarious punishment affecting motivation
Cultivation through years of exposure
Agenda setting through issue salience
Prior restraint by government
quizQuestions.answer: Vicarious punishment affecting motivation
quizQuestions.explanation: Observed punishment can reduce motivation to reproduce a learned behavior even when the viewer attended to and retained it.

quizQuestions.question: When many reporters follow the same story and use similar professional news judgments, the pattern is called:
options: Pack journalism
Prior restraint
Vicarious reinforcement
Symbolic annihilation
quizQuestions.answer: Pack journalism
quizQuestions.explanation: Shared news values and routines can lead reporters to pursue and present similar stories, a pattern commonly called pack journalism.

quizQuestions.question: Calling the press a “watchdog” or “fourth estate” emphasizes its role in:
options: Monitoring government and informing the public about wrongdoing
Electing judges directly
Replacing legislatures in making law
Guaranteeing that every report is unbiased
quizQuestions.answer: Monitoring government and informing the public about wrongdoing
quizQuestions.explanation: The watchdog ideal treats an independent press as a check that investigates public power and gives citizens information needed for accountability.

quizQuestions.question: Media's agenda-setting role in elections means that:
options: Media directly tells voters which candidate to support
The issues media emphasizes tend to become the issues voters consider most important
Politicians' actual policies are always the most covered election topics
Social media has replaced traditional media in setting the political agenda
quizQuestions.answer: The issues media emphasizes tend to become the issues voters consider most important
quizQuestions.explanation: In elections, media coverage patterns shape which policy issues voters prioritize — issues receiving heavy coverage become more salient in voters' minds when evaluating candidates.

quizQuestions.question: Two outlets cover the same housing proposal, but one stresses affordability while the other stresses traffic disruption. This most directly illustrates:
options: Framing
Direct government censorship
Vicarious punishment
Perfectly uniform audience effects
quizQuestions.answer: Framing
quizQuestions.explanation: Framing changes how an issue is presented by emphasizing different aspects, causes, or consequences.

quizQuestions.question: Short response: What is media gatekeeping?
quizQuestions.answer: Media gatekeeping is the process of selecting, filtering, and prioritizing which information or stories reach an audience.
quizQuestions.explanation: A complete response identifies selection or filtering and explains that visibility and prominence influence what audiences encounter.

quizQuestions.question: Consumer culture refers to a social system in which:
options: Consumers have legal protections from corporate exploitation
Identity, social status, and meaning are primarily constructed through purchasing and owning goods
Citizens are educated to resist advertising manipulation
The government controls what goods are produced and sold
quizQuestions.answer: Identity, social status, and meaning are primarily constructed through purchasing and owning goods
quizQuestions.explanation: Consumer culture is a social and economic system in which identity, status, and fulfillment are primarily achieved through acquiring and displaying consumer goods — heavily maintained by advertising.

quizQuestions.question: The concept of 'manufactured demand' in advertising refers to:
options: Using factory production to reduce the cost of advertised goods
Creating desire for products that consumers did not previously feel they needed
Measuring actual consumer demand through market research
Manufacturing advertising materials in foreign countries to reduce costs
quizQuestions.answer: Creating desire for products that consumers did not previously feel they needed
quizQuestions.explanation: Advertising often creates or manufactures demand — using emotional appeals, social comparison, and aspirational imagery to make people feel they need products they were unaware they wanted.

quizQuestions.question: An advertisement sells a watch by showing status, travel, and admiration rather than explaining timekeeping. This is primarily:
options: Lifestyle advertising
Public-service communication
Product recall
Prior restraint
quizQuestions.answer: Lifestyle advertising
quizQuestions.explanation: Lifestyle advertising links a product to an aspirational identity or emotional state rather than only to functional features.

quizQuestions.question: Short response: Define or explain: Lifestyle advertising connects products to.
quizQuestions.answer: Lifestyle advertising connects products to desired identities, emotions, social status, values, or ways of living rather than only to practical features.
quizQuestions.explanation: The appeal works by suggesting what kind of person the consumer can become or signal by buying the product.

quizQuestions.question: The term 'hegemonic masculinity' in media studies refers to:
options: The statistical dominance of male characters in media
The dominant cultural ideal of masculinity promoted in mainstream media as the standard men should meet
Legal discrimination against men in the entertainment industry
The use of male actors to portray historically male roles
quizQuestions.answer: The dominant cultural ideal of masculinity promoted in mainstream media as the standard men should meet
quizQuestions.explanation: Hegemonic masculinity describes the dominant, idealized form of masculinity (strong, emotionally restrained, powerful, heterosexual) that mainstream media promotes and that men are expected to aspire to.

quizQuestions.question: Research on media and body image has found that exposure to idealized body images in media:
options: Has no measurable effect on audience body satisfaction
Is associated with increased body dissatisfaction, particularly among women and girls
Consistently motivates healthy diet and exercise behaviors
Only affects people who already have body image concerns
quizQuestions.answer: Is associated with increased body dissatisfaction, particularly among women and girls
quizQuestions.explanation: Extensive research links exposure to idealized body images in advertising and entertainment to decreased body satisfaction, disordered eating behaviors, and lower self-esteem.

quizQuestions.question: The term 'femvertising' refers to advertising that:
options: Is produced by and for female-owned businesses
Uses feminist messages and female empowerment to sell products
Targets exclusively female consumers with traditional gender imagery
Shows women in traditional domestic roles to appeal to homemakers
quizQuestions.answer: Uses feminist messages and female empowerment to sell products
quizQuestions.explanation: Femvertising is a marketing strategy that uses feminist themes, empowerment messaging, and positive female representation to build brand image and appeal to female consumers.

quizQuestions.question: Which portrayal most clearly challenges a gender stereotype?
options: A father and daughter share technical and household tasks without treating either as unusual
Only boys are shown building robots
A car ad equates masculinity with aggression
A cleaning ad shows women as naturally responsible for all housework
quizQuestions.answer: A father and daughter share technical and household tasks without treating either as unusual
quizQuestions.explanation: The portrayal distributes competence and care across genders instead of reinforcing a narrow role expectation.

questions.question: Harold Lasswell identified which three functions of mass media?
options: Entertainment, advertising, and propaganda
Surveillance, correlation, and cultural transmission
Gatekeeping, framing, and agenda-setting
Production, distribution, and consumption
questions.answer: Surveillance, correlation, and cultural transmission
questions.explanation: Lasswell identified surveillance (monitoring the environment), correlation (interpreting events), and cultural transmission (passing on social norms and values) as core media functions.

questions.question: Media literacy involves all of the following EXCEPT:
options: Analyzing who created a media message
Evaluating what techniques are used to attract attention
Accepting all media messages from established outlets without question
Identifying what values or viewpoints are represented or absent
questions.answer: Accepting all media messages from established outlets without question
questions.explanation: Media literacy requires critical evaluation of ALL media messages, including those from established outlets — uncritical acceptance is the opposite of media literacy.

questions.question: According to agenda-setting theory, media's most powerful influence is on:
options: What audiences think about specific issues
Which issues audiences consider important
How audiences vote in elections
What products audiences purchase
questions.answer: Which issues audiences consider important
questions.explanation: Agenda-setting proposes that media influences issue salience — which topics the public considers most important — rather than directly determining specific opinions or behaviors.

questions.question: Cultivation theory's 'mean world syndrome' predicts that heavy, long-term exposure to televised violence may lead viewers to:
options: Perceive the world as more dangerous than available evidence suggests
Ignore every violent message because audiences are always active
Copy any behavior immediately after one exposure
Become better at estimating official crime statistics
questions.answer: Perceive the world as more dangerous than available evidence suggests
questions.explanation: Cultivation theory concerns gradual worldview effects from repeated exposure; it does not claim every viewer responds identically or imitates immediately.

questions.question: In Bandura's Social Learning Theory, 'modeling' refers to:
options: Creating fashion content for social media
Imitating behaviors observed in others, including media figures
Designing research studies on media effects
Formally teaching behaviors through structured instruction
questions.answer: Imitating behaviors observed in others, including media figures
questions.explanation: Modeling is the process of observing and imitating behaviors displayed by others — a key mechanism through which media can influence audience attitudes and behaviors.

questions.question: The framing of the same immigration story as either a 'crisis' or an 'opportunity' demonstrates:
options: Balanced journalism presenting both sides of an issue
How word and image choices shape audience interpretation of events
The agenda-setting power to determine which issues are covered
The objectivity required by professional journalism standards
questions.answer: How word and image choices shape audience interpretation of events
questions.explanation: Framing the same event with different language, images, and emphasis shapes how audiences interpret and emotionally respond to the issue — a demonstration of framing theory.

questions.question: Media's role in consumer culture is primarily to:
questions.answer: Media's role in consumer culture is to circulate advertising and stories that connect goods and brands with identity, desire, status, and everyday habits.
questions.explanation: A strong answer explains that media do more than announce products; they help make consumption meaningful in social life.

questions.question: What does the Bechdel Test check in a film?
options: Whether at least two named women talk to each other about something other than a man
Whether a woman directed the film and plays the lead
Whether women receive equal screen time in every scene
Whether the film avoids every gender stereotype
questions.answer: Whether at least two named women talk to each other about something other than a man
questions.explanation: The test is a limited screen-representation indicator; passing it does not by itself prove a film is equitable or free of stereotypes.

questions.question: Symbolic annihilation in media, as described by Gaye Tuchman, refers to:
options: Violence against symbolic characters in video games
The rendering of certain groups invisible through absence or trivialization in media
Censoring historically offensive media content
The decline of symbolic storytelling in modern media
questions.answer: The rendering of certain groups invisible through absence or trivialization in media
questions.explanation: Symbolic annihilation describes how groups are effectively made invisible or insignificant in media through underrepresentation, stereotyping, or trivializing their portrayals.

questions.question: Confirmation bias in media consumption describes the tendency to:
options: Confirm whether media sources have been fact-checked before trusting them
Seek out information that reinforces existing beliefs and reject contradicting information
Read multiple sources before forming any opinion
Confirm the identity of journalists before trusting their reporting
questions.answer: Seek out information that reinforces existing beliefs and reject contradicting information
questions.explanation: Confirmation bias leads people to favor media content that confirms their pre-existing beliefs and to discount, avoid, or dismiss information that challenges those beliefs.

questions.question: Horse race journalism in election coverage prioritizes:
options: Policy analysis and candidate qualifications
Poll standings, momentum, and competition rather than substantive policy differences
Investigation of campaign finance and donor influence
Equal coverage of all registered candidates
questions.answer: Poll standings, momentum, and competition rather than substantive policy differences
questions.explanation: Horse race journalism focuses on who is ahead in polls and the competitive dynamics of campaigns rather than the substantive policy positions and qualifications of candidates.

questions.question: The hypodermic-needle model assumes that media messages:
options: Directly and powerfully affect largely passive audiences
Have no influence unless audiences already agree
Only affect audiences through long-term cultivation
Are interpreted identically because of government regulation
questions.answer: Directly and powerfully affect largely passive audiences
questions.explanation: This early model treats effects as direct and uniform; later research gives audiences and social context a more active role.

questions.question: Which conclusion best reflects current evidence about social media use and adolescent mental health?
options: Some patterns of use are associated with worse outcomes for some adolescents, but effects vary and observational studies do not by themselves prove causation
Social media use causes depression in every adolescent
Social media consistently improves mental health for all users
Researchers have found no relationship worth studying
questions.answer: Some patterns of use are associated with worse outcomes for some adolescents, but effects vary and observational studies do not by themselves prove causation
questions.explanation: The evidence is heterogeneous: associations depend on type of use, individual vulnerability, context, and measurement, and correlation alone cannot establish causation.

questions.question: Surveillance capitalism (Zuboff) refers to an economic system where:
questions.answer: Surveillance capitalism refers to an economic system where personal data and behavioral traces are collected, analyzed, and monetized to predict or influence behavior.
questions.explanation: The concept focuses on data extraction as a business model, especially when users have limited understanding or control over how their data is used.

questions.question: Which condition most directly weakens a local newsroom’s ability to perform sustained watchdog reporting?
options: Too many journalists working in investigative reporting
Financial pressures that cause newsrooms to close or cut investigative staff
Government prohibiting journalists from publishing news at all
Audiences spending too much time reading news
questions.answer: Financial pressures that cause newsrooms to close or cut investigative staff
questions.explanation: Loss of reporting staff and resources reduces time for records requests, source development, and investigations; the item avoids claiming that one cause is always the single greatest threat.

questions.question: A news outlet repeatedly describes a housing proposal with the attributes “urgent,” “high-density,” and “tax-saving.” This is an example of second-level agenda-setting because it:
options: Shapes which attributes audiences associate with the issue
Determines whether the issue appears anywhere in the news
Proves audiences will support the proposal
Measures how many minutes people watch
questions.answer: Shapes which attributes audiences associate with the issue
questions.explanation: Second-level agenda-setting emphasizes which attributes or frames become salient, while first-level agenda-setting emphasizes which issues receive attention.

questions.question: Cultivation Theory predicts that media effects are strongest for which type of audience?
options: Light viewers who watch TV occasionally
Heavy, long-term viewers who consume large amounts of similar content
Young children who watch educational programming
Highly educated adults who consume diverse media
questions.answer: Heavy, long-term viewers who consume large amounts of similar content
questions.explanation: Cultivation Theory predicts that effects accumulate through heavy, long-term, consistent exposure — making heavy television viewers most susceptible to cultivated worldview beliefs.

questions.question: For social learning from media to lead to behavior change, Bandura's model requires all of the following EXCEPT:
options: Attention to the modeled behavior
Retention (memory) of the behavior
Direct personal experience with consequences of the behavior
Motivation to reproduce the behavior
questions.answer: Direct personal experience with consequences of the behavior
questions.explanation: Social learning can occur without direct personal experience with consequences — observing a model being rewarded or punished is sufficient motivation for learning.

questions.question: Media filter bubbles in political contexts are most likely to lead to:
options: Greater understanding of opposing political viewpoints
Increased political polarization as people receive only perspective-confirming information
More accurate political information as algorithms remove false content
Greater civic engagement through shared media experiences
questions.answer: Increased political polarization as people receive only perspective-confirming information
questions.explanation: Filter bubbles expose people primarily to content that confirms existing political beliefs, potentially reinforcing extreme positions and reducing exposure to compromise or alternative perspectives.

questions.question: Which example best illustrates symbolic annihilation?
options: A social group is consistently absent or trivialized across popular media
A film uses a white actor in a role associated with a person of color
A journalist corrects a mistaken caption
An advertisement targets a narrow age group
questions.answer: A social group is consistently absent or trivialized across popular media
questions.explanation: Symbolic annihilation refers to erasure through omission, condemnation, or trivialization; whitewashing can contribute but is a narrower casting practice.

questions.question: Research linking social media use to body dissatisfaction primarily involves the mechanism of:
questions.answer: The primary mechanism is social comparison, especially comparison with idealized, edited, or selectively presented bodies and lifestyles.
questions.explanation: The answer should focus on how repeated comparison to curated images can shape self-evaluation, not simply on social media use by itself.

questions.question: Disinformation campaigns on social media are most effective because they:
options: Use complex arguments that are difficult for ordinary people to evaluate
Exploit emotional resonance, confirmation bias, and algorithmic amplification to spread rapidly
Are backed by scientific data that appears credible
Can only be spread by government-sponsored accounts with large followings
questions.answer: Exploit emotional resonance, confirmation bias, and algorithmic amplification to spread rapidly
questions.explanation: Disinformation exploits emotional triggers and confirmation bias, and is amplified by algorithms optimizing for engagement — making it spread faster and wider than factual corrections.

questions.question: News deserts harm democracy primarily because they:
options: Force citizens to rely exclusively on entertainment for information
Leave communities without local accountability journalism to monitor government, schools, and businesses
Create too much competition among the remaining news outlets
Encourage citizens to trust social media as their primary news source
questions.answer: Leave communities without local accountability journalism to monitor government, schools, and businesses
questions.explanation: When local newsrooms close, communities lose coverage of local government, school boards, and businesses — creating information vacuums that enable corruption and reduce civic accountability.

questions.question: Before sharing a startling AI-generated video, which response best applies media-literacy principles?
options: Locate the earliest source, inspect provenance and context, and seek independent corroboration
Share it first and correct it later if necessary
Trust it if the account has many followers
Assume every synthetic-looking clip is false
questions.answer: Locate the earliest source, inspect provenance and context, and seek independent corroboration
questions.explanation: Verification should combine source tracing, provenance/context checks, and corroboration; appearance or popularity alone is not reliable evidence.

questions.question: The creator economy has democratized media production by:
options: Eliminating the need for any quality standards in media content
Enabling individuals to produce and distribute content directly to global audiences without institutional gatekeepers
Creating new government regulations that make media production easier
Reducing the total number of media sources available to audiences
questions.answer: Enabling individuals to produce and distribute content directly to global audiences without institutional gatekeepers
questions.explanation: The creator economy empowers individuals to bypass traditional media gatekeepers (studios, publishers, networks) and directly reach audiences through YouTube, Substack, podcasts, and social platforms.

questions.question: Herman and Chomsky’s propaganda model argues that structural pressures on commercial news can:
options: Narrow routine news framing toward perspectives compatible with powerful corporate and political institutions
Prove that every journalist deliberately fabricates stories
Show that one secret organization controls all media content
Eliminate disagreement among news organizations
questions.answer: Narrow routine news framing toward perspectives compatible with powerful corporate and political institutions
questions.explanation: The propaganda model is a critical theory about ownership, advertising, sourcing, and other institutional filters; it does not claim that all journalists consciously coordinate or falsify news.

questions.question: What does end-to-end encryption protect most directly?
options: Message content in transit so only endpoint devices hold the decryption keys
All metadata, device security, and participant identity automatically
Users from every phishing attempt
Messages after an unlocked recipient device displays them
questions.answer: Message content in transit so only endpoint devices hold the decryption keys
questions.explanation: End-to-end encryption protects message content from intermediaries, but it does not by itself hide all metadata, secure compromised endpoints, or authenticate every participant.

questions.question: Prior restraint — government preventing publication before it occurs — is most clearly prohibited by:
questions.answer: In the United States, prior restraint is most clearly prohibited by the First Amendment's protection of freedom of speech and freedom of the press.
questions.explanation: The concept concerns government blocking publication before it happens, which is treated as a severe threat to press freedom.

questions.question: Lifestyle advertising is most effective at selling because it:
options: Provides detailed information about product features and price
Associates products with aspirational identities, social groups, and emotional states
Uses scientific endorsements from independent research institutions
Compares the product favorably to all competing alternatives
questions.answer: Associates products with aspirational identities, social groups, and emotional states
questions.explanation: Lifestyle advertising sells not just a product but a desired identity — making consumers feel that purchasing the product will bring them closer to the social group, status, or emotional state depicted.

questions.question: Racial stereotyping in media is most harmful when:
options: It appears only in historical dramas set in the past
It is repeated consistently across many media platforms, normalizing and reinforcing biased perceptions
It is challenged by other characters within the same program
It is clearly labeled as fiction and not based on real people
questions.answer: It is repeated consistently across many media platforms, normalizing and reinforcing biased perceptions
questions.explanation: The harmful effects of racial stereotyping are cumulative — consistent repetition across multiple media normalizes biased perceptions, shaping both audience attitudes toward stereotyped groups and how those groups see themselves.

questions.question: FOMO (Fear of Missing Out) as a social media effect refers to:
options: Anxiety about losing access to social media accounts
Anxiety caused by social comparison with curated images of peers' social lives
Fear of being left behind technologically as new platforms emerge
Concern about missing breaking news by not checking social media constantly
questions.answer: Anxiety caused by social comparison with curated images of peers' social lives
questions.explanation: FOMO is the anxiety driven by social comparison — seeing others' seemingly exciting, socially rich lives on social media creates feelings of inadequacy and exclusion.

questions.question: Which statement best describes a democratic role of independent media?
options: They can inform citizens, scrutinize power, and support public debate
They must endorse one official national viewpoint
They guarantee that every audience member reaches the same conclusion
They replace elections and courts as decision makers
questions.answer: They can inform citizens, scrutinize power, and support public debate
questions.explanation: Independent media can support accountability and deliberation, but media reports do not replace civic institutions and do not guarantee uniform audience effects.

questions.question: The difference between objective reporting and advocacy journalism is:
options: Objective reporting is always more accurate than advocacy journalism
Objective journalism aims for neutrality while advocacy journalism openly promotes a particular perspective or cause
Advocacy journalism is always funded by political organizations
Only objective journalism is protected by the First Amendment
questions.answer: Objective journalism aims for neutrality while advocacy journalism openly promotes a particular perspective or cause
questions.explanation: Objective journalism strives for impartiality and neutrality, while advocacy journalism openly identifies a viewpoint and works to advance it — both are legal under the First Amendment but differ in editorial philosophy.

questions.question: Intersectionality as a framework for analyzing media representation considers how:
options: Multiple media platforms intersect to create a unified media ecosystem
Race, gender, class, and other identities overlap to create distinct representation experiences
Film, TV, and digital media intersect in the contemporary media landscape
International and domestic media create intersecting cultural influences
questions.answer: Race, gender, class, and other identities overlap to create distinct representation experiences
questions.explanation: Intersectionality, developed by Kimberlé Crenshaw, examines how overlapping social identities (race, gender, class, sexuality) interact to shape distinct experiences of representation, privilege, and discrimination in media.

questions.question: Which of the following best exemplifies responsible digital citizenship in an age of misinformation?
questions.answer: Responsible digital citizenship means checking source credibility, comparing claims with reliable evidence, reading beyond headlines, and avoiding the spread of unverified information.
questions.explanation: The answer should emphasize verification and restraint: digital citizens help reduce misinformation instead of amplifying it.
